subtype: Approach: commit gradually because each step seemed small [Pitfall]
passage: You asked why I never say "just try one session", Devika. Let me tell you. I'm Ishita. I was twenty. A classmate invited me to a free workshop on confidence, and it was lovely. The next month there was a small donation for the hall. Then a larger one for study materials. Then the group needed me on weekdays, and I told myself college could wait a semester. Each step felt like only a little more than the last, so I never saw the staircase I was climbing. The day my mother came to the group's house and asked me to walk home, I stood there and could not explain how I had got there. It took me a year to leave, and my savings never came back.

qa.q: What was the first thing the classmate offered Ishita?
qa.a: The classmate offered a free workshop on confidence.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when the mother asked to walk home?
qa.a: Ishita felt stuck and embarrassed, unable to explain how things had gone so far.

qa.q: At which point in the story could Ishita have stopped, and why?
qa.a: Ishita could have stopped at the first donation, when a free workshop turned into a request for money, because that was the earliest clear change.

qa.q: How did Ishita's mother see the situation at the group's house?
qa.a: Ishita's mother was probably frightened and heartbroken, standing in a stranger's house and asking Ishita to come home.

grounding: Illustrates joining a group through small steps, from a free workshop to donations and leaving college, where each step seemed consistent with the last.

subtype: Approach: commit gradually because each step seemed small [Pitfall]
passage:
It started with a free workshop at a Hyderabad hotel, on a rainy Sunday when Mohit had nothing else to do. The speaker was brilliant. The next week there was a small "contribution" for the follow-up session. Then a weekend retreat, which cost more. Each step felt like the obvious next thing.
By March, the group asked him to volunteer every evening. He started missing lectures. His friend Ankita messaged, "Are you okay? You've missed three lab submissions."
"I'm fine," he wrote. "This matters more."
In April the group leader said Mohit was "ready for full-time service", which meant leaving college. His semester fees were due in a week. He gave the leader his fee money instead as a "commitment".
When he finally sat in his hostel room one night and added it all up, he couldn't believe he'd got here. Every step had been so small. He picked up his phone and called his father.

qa.q: What did Mohit give the leader instead of paying his semester fees?
qa.a: He gave his fee money as a 'commitment'.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when he added it all up in his hostel room?
qa.a: He felt shocked and disbelieving, unable to believe how far the small steps had taken him.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Mohit handled the group's requests?
qa.a: I would set a firm limit at the first paid step and talk to Ankita or family before each new commitment, so no step could quietly lead to the next.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the changes in Mohit?
qa.a: Ankita notices missed lab submissions and is worried, but feels shut out when he says the group matters more.

grounding: Shows the person moving from a free workshop to donations to leaving college, each step small, until the escalating commitment makes leaving hard.

subtype: Approach: commit gradually because each step seemed small [Pitfall]
passage:
Kavitha's first visit was a free Friday meditation at a hall in Chennai's Anna Nagar. It felt peaceful. Next came a Sunday course, "just a small fee". Then a monthly donation, "to keep the light going". She agreed each time; saying no felt like going back on what she'd already done.
By the third month she was at the hall every evening. Her college attendance dropped. The leader suggested she "stop wasting time on a degree that won't free you" and help the group full time.
Her classmate Eshaan found her outside the library one afternoon. "You haven't been in class for two weeks. Your mother called me."
Kavitha felt a jolt. She hadn't called her mother in a month. The leader had said family were "old ties".
"I only meant to go to one meditation," she said slowly. Eshaan waited. That evening she called her mother and, for the first time, didn't go to the hall.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha's first visit take place?
qa.a: At a hall in Chennai's Anna Nagar.

qa.q: What did Kavitha feel when Eshaan said her mother had called him?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of shock and guilt, realising she hadn't called her mother in a month.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do to step back safely?
qa.a: She could keep talking with her mother and Eshaan and ask the college counsellor for support, so she isn't facing the group's pressure alone.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's mother have felt before calling Eshaan?
qa.a: Her mother was likely worried and frightened, not hearing from her daughter for a month.

grounding: Shows the person moving step by step from a free session to fees, donations and dropping college, with each small step making leaving harder.
